Chapter 1: Facing Mortality in Everyday Life
Ever have one of those quiet moments, right in the middle of a hectic day, when it suddenly hits you—everything ends, even this? Most of the time, we just brush the thought aside. There’s always another errand to run, something urgent at work, or some little crisis to steal our attention. But, deep down, that awareness—that life is finite—never really leaves us. It lingers in the background, quietly shaping the way we make choices and how we feel, even if we don’t always realize it. This isn’t just some big philosophical riddle. It’s like a silent companion that’s always there, coloring the way we see ourselves and the world around us. Picture a child, just beginning to understand that pets don’t live forever. One morning, the family goldfish isn’t swimming anymore. The questions start pouring in—why did this happen? Will it happen to everyone? The grown-ups try to offer gentle answers, but the kid senses something bigger, something even the adults can’t quite explain. That first brush with loss plants a tiny seed. And as the years go by, it grows quietly in the background. As we get older, our awareness of death changes and deepens. Think about a teenager, frustrated with the endless rules and routines of school. There’s this urge to do something that matters—to stand out, to be remembered. Sound familiar? That drive isn’t just about ego or ambition. It’s a way of pushing back against the uncomfortable truth that our time is limited. The desire to leave a legacy, to be a hero in some way, is really about wanting to matter, even after we’re gone. But here’s the thing: most adults don’t talk openly about death. The subject comes up in whispers at funerals, or during a crisis, but rarely in everyday conversation. Instead, we build routines, chase after achievements, invest in relationships. It might seem like these things are just about happiness or success, but really, they’re about creating meaning. We use our routines as a kind of shield, protecting ourselves from the anxiety that comes with knowing everything is temporary. Society tries to help, too. Cultural traditions, religious beliefs, and shared stories offer comfort, promising that life goes on in some way. These systems make us feel like we belong to something bigger—something that lasts beyond any one person. Whether it’s the hope of an afterlife, the pride we feel in our communities, or the satisfaction of helping a cause, these beliefs give us a bit of security. Still, the fear never really disappears. It sneaks up in different ways—maybe it’s anxiety before making a big decision, a sudden emptiness after reaching a goal you’ve chased for years, or that quiet panic that comes with illness or aging. Most of us don’t realize these feelings are connected to a deeper awareness of mortality. Instead, we look for distractions, hoping we can outrun that discomfort. Some people try to take control. They plan every detail, organize their lives down to the last minute, and try to predict every possible outcome. Others go the opposite way—breaking the rules, chasing thrills, acting almost as if danger can make them invincible. But at the core, both are really just different ways of trying to manage the fear, to grab a sense of power over what we can’t control. And then, in those quieter moments, the truth is impossible to ignore. A parent watches their child grow up, a worker nears retirement, or a friend says goodbye at a hospital bedside. We’re reminded, in the most personal way, that time moves on—no matter what we wish or plan. The real challenge isn’t just to accept that reality, but to figure out how to live with it, to find some peace with the limits of our existence. Most of us don’t see how much of what we do is shaped by our denial of death. The drive to achieve, the need to be recognized, the constant search for meaning—they’re all ways of coping with the fact that life is fragile. So, here’s what really matters: recognize how this awareness influences your choices and relationships. Try to live honestly, even in the shadow of mortality.
